title: House and Smile
premise: Quentin Iversen, a pest controller who prides himself on believing only in what he can spray, is called to his late grandmother's house where every photograph now shows an extra chair—and sometimes an extra person, blurred, smiling. The house remembers a crime the town buried: a lodger who vanished in 1974, and the family who sang to keep him quiet. As the chair follows Quentin home through photographs, mirrors, and finally memory itself, he must recover the song's forbidden last verse—the one that names the dead—without singing along and becoming part of the house. In the end, Quentin chooses justice over survival: he speaks the verse aloud at the ruined house, freeing the lodger's ghost but forfeiting his own invisibility, and walks out of the story as the next blurred figure in other people's photographs.
about_author: Coral Brightwater is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing estate-sale photographs and swears three of them changed while she watched. She writes horror from a farmhouse in coastal Maine that she refuses to photograph.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Quentin takes a routine pest-control job at his grandmother's shuttered house, annoyed more than unsettled by the scratching in the walls. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: dry skepticism establishing his armor of disbelief.

chapters.title: Something With Fingerprints
chapters.summary: In the attic Quentin finds greasy handprints climbing the rafters—too large, too human, arranged like someone climbing toward help. He logs it as raccoon damage. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: first hairline crack in his disbelief.

chapters.title: Extra Seating
chapters.summary: Sorting grandma's photos for the estate sale, Quentin notices a wooden chair in every image, including shots taken outdoors. His cousin Dana insists it was always there. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: creeping gaslight dread.

chapters.title: The Lodger File
chapters.summary: Quentin digs into family boxes and finds a 1974 missing-persons clipping: boarder Elias Vann, gone without a trace. Grandma's handwriting on the margin reads 'we sang.' POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Dana Knows the Tune
chapters.summary: Dana hums a lullaby she can't remember learning; Quentin recognizes it from the attic night. When she stops mid-verse, her nose bleeds. POV: Dana. Emotional beat: inherited guilt surfacing through the body.

chapters.title: Chair in the Corridor
chapters.summary: Quentin returns alone and finds the chair physically present in the hallway, warm to the touch, facing his grandmother's bedroom door. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: denial's last stand against evidence he can touch.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Won't Say
chapters.summary: An elderly neighbor, Mrs. Okonkwo, tells him the whole street heard singing the week Elias vanished, and that the Iversens never sang again after. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: the horror of a town's polite silence.

chapters.title: Verse One, Verse Two
chapters.summary: Quentin finds sheet music hidden in grandma's hymnal—the lullaby, two verses only, the third torn out. That night he dreams the melody and wakes with sore throat. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: the song claiming him.

chapters.title: Photographs of the Living
chapters.summary: New photos on Quentin's own phone now include the chair behind him, closer each time. He smashes the phone; the chair appears in his apartment window reflection anyway. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: isolation as the haunting goes viral in his life.

chapters.title: Dana's Confession
chapters.summary: Dana reveals grandma made the children sing to Elias 'so he'd sleep' during his final week—he was sick, not violent, and they kept him locked in. She was five. POV: Dana. Emotional beat: shame passed down like furniture.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Out Loud
chapters.summary: At the house, walls sweat and whisper the lullaby in grandma's voice; Quentin records it and hears a fourth voice underneath, hoarse, asking to be named. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: pity replacing fear.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Warning
chapters.summary: The neighbor explains the rule: the last verse names the dead, but whoever sings it joins them. Her own brother tried in 1980; there's a chair in her hallway too. POV: Mrs. Okonkwo. Emotional beat: the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Torn Page
chapters.summary: Quentin tracks the torn hymnal page to a burned church archive and recovers a scorched fragment: half a line, ending in Elias's initial. The chair appears in his rearview mirror. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: hope sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: The Town That Sang
chapters.summary: Quentin canvasses old residents; each household has its own extra chair, its own buried wrong. The haunting isn't a curse—it's a ledger. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: justice outside the law taking shape.

chapters.title: Dana Disappears
chapters.summary: Dana stops answering calls; Quentin finds her car outside the house and inside finds her seated in the chair, humming, eyes open, half-gone into the wallpaper's pattern. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: terror fused with responsibility.

chapters.title: Singing Along
chapters.summary: To reach Dana, Quentin enters the house's remembered 1974, walking through a replayed week, nearly harmonizing before biting his tongue bloody. He drags Dana out; she doesn't recognize him. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: sacrifice without resolution.

chapters.title: The Missing Line
chapters.summary: Grandma's lawyer delivers a sealed letter: the full last verse, written before her death, with instructions never to open it unless someone sits in the chair. Someone has. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: the trap closing gently.

chapters.title: Naming Elias
chapters.summary: The letter names not just Elias but everyone who let him die—including grandma, including the town, including, in a postscript, whoever reads aloud. Quentin understands the choice is real. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: moral clarity at the worst possible cost.

chapters.title: Last Verse
chapters.summary: At midnight in the house, Quentin sings the final verse—naming Elias Vann, refusing to name himself—altering the cadence so the song ends on accusation instead of invitation. The house screams. Climax. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: courage as deliberate self-destruction.

chapters.title: Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Dana wakes whole; the chairs vanish from every photograph in town; Elias's presence lifts like weather. But Quentin's reflection lags now, and his own phone photos blur where he stands. POV: Dana. Emotional beat: relief shadowed by loss.

chapters.title: The Price
chapters.summary: Quentin fades from records, memories, and Dana's recognition over one long autumn, staying just long enough to burn the house down properly and leave the truth in a public archive. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: House and Smile
chapters.summary: Years later, Dana receives an anonymous photo of her new home: on the porch, a blurred smiling man beside an empty chair, watching over her. She smiles back and does not sing. Resolution. POV: Dana. Emotional beat: haunted peace—survival remembered, justice kept.
